resultative_so_such_that.name: Resultative Degree Constructions (So + Adj / Such + NP + that ...)

A1_A2.pedagogical_function: Highlights how strong a quality or feeling is ('so... that...' / 'such... that...') and shows the result that follows.
A1_A2.imitation_example: The freshman practiced his speech so carefully that he answered every question with confidence.
A1_A2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (So vs. Such before Adjectives/Adverbs vs. Noun Phrases): Learners frequently confuse 'so + Adj/Adv' with 'such + (a/an) + Adj + Noun': "The course was [INCORRECT: such difficult -> CORRECT: so difficult] that many students asked for extra tutoring." (Note: Use 'so' before an adjective or adverb alone, and 'such' before a noun phrase).

variants.imitation_example: The freshman practiced his speech so carefully that he answered every question with confidence.
variants.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (So vs. Such before Adjectives/Adverbs & Quantifiers): Learners frequently use 'such' instead of 'so' before an adjective, adverb, or 'much/many': "He struggled [INCORRECT: such much -> CORRECT: so much] in the first-semester physics class that he visited the tutor every week." (Note: Always use 'so' before an adjective, adverb, or quantity word like 'much/many/little/few').

variants.imitation_example: The speaker told such an inspiring story that the whole class clapped warmly.
variants.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (So vs. Such before Noun Phrases): Learners frequently confuse 'so + Adj' with 'such + (a/an) + Adj + Noun': "It was [INCORRECT: so a helpful lesson -> CORRECT: such a helpful lesson] that every student remembered it." (Note: Use 'so' before an adjective or adverb alone, and 'such' before a noun phrase).

B1_B2.pedagogical_function: Intensifies an attribute or situation ('so + [Adj/Adv] + that...' / 'such + [NP] + that...') to foreground its consequential impact.
B1_B2.imitation_example: The introductory engineering course was so demanding that several freshmen reconsidered their academic major.
B1_B2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (So vs. Such with Quantifiers & Uncountable Nouns): Learners frequently use 'such' before 'many/much/few/little' or add 'a/an' before uncountable nouns after 'such': "The platform generated [INCORRECT: such many user requests / such a rapid progress -> CORRECT: so many user requests / such rapid progress] that the servers had to be upgraded." (Note: Use 'so' before quantity determiners 'many/much/few/little', and omit 'a/an' when 'such' precedes an uncountable or plural noun).

variants.imitation_example: The introductory engineering course was so demanding that several freshmen reconsidered their academic major.
variants.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (So vs. Such with Quantifiers & Uncountable Nouns): Learners frequently use 'such' before 'many/much/few/little' or before standalone adjectives/adverbs: "The platform generated [INCORRECT: such many user requests -> CORRECT: so many user requests] that the servers had to be upgraded." (Note: Use 'so' before adjectives, adverbs, and quantity determiners 'many/much/few/little').

variants.imitation_example: The documentary presented such compelling evidence of ocean plastic pollution that three coastal cities banned disposable foam containers.
variants.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Such + Uncountable / Plural Noun Phrases): Learners frequently insert 'a/an' after 'such' before uncountable nouns or use 'so' before a full noun phrase: "The research team made [INCORRECT: such a rapid progress / so rapid progress -> CORRECT: such rapid progress] that the clinical trial launched ahead of schedule." (Note: Use 'such' without 'a/an' before uncountable or plural noun phrases).

C1_C2.pedagogical_function: Builds rhetorical intensity by scaling an adjectival or nominal predicate ('so + [Adj/Adv] + that...' / 'So + [Adj] + [be] + [Subject] + that...') to underscore a transformative consequence.
C1_C2.imitation_example: His critique of institutional speciesism was so incisive and empirically grounded that it reshaped university ethics curricula worldwide.
C1_C2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Fronted 'So / Such' Degree Inversion & Article Placement): Learners frequently fail to invert the copula/auxiliary when 'So + [Adj]' or 'Such' is fronted for rhetorical emphasis, or misplace the article in 'so + [Adj] + a + [Singular Noun]': "So decisive [INCORRECT: the consumer boycott was -> CORRECT: was the consumer boycott] that rival cosmetics conglomerates abandoned live testing within months." (Note: Fronting 'So + [Adj/Adv]' or 'Such + [be]' at the start of a clause requires subject-auxiliary inversion before the 'that'-result clause).

variants.imitation_example: His critique of institutional speciesism was so incisive and empirically grounded that it reshaped university ethics curricula worldwide.
variants.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Fronted 'So / Such' Degree Inversion & Article Placement): Learners frequently fail to invert the copula/auxiliary when 'So + [Adj]' or 'Such' is fronted for rhetorical emphasis, or misplace the article in 'so + [Adj] + a + [Singular Noun]': "So decisive [INCORRECT: the consumer boycott was -> CORRECT: was the consumer boycott] that rival cosmetics conglomerates abandoned live testing within months." (Note: Fronting 'So + [Adj/Adv]' or 'Such + [be]' at the start of a clause requires subject-auxiliary inversion before the 'that'-result clause).

variants.imitation_example: The investigative expose triggered such widespread public backlash that multinational conglomerates overhauled their testing policies within months.
variants.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning ('Such' vs. 'So + Adj + a/an + Singular Noun'): Learners frequently misorder the article when converting 'such a/an + Adj + Noun' into the formal 'so + Adj + a/an + Noun' frame: "The campaign posed [INCORRECT: so a formidable challenge / such formidable challenge -> CORRECT: such a formidable challenge / so formidable a challenge] that industry lobbyists conceded." (Note: Place 'a/an' after 'such' ['such a formidable challenge'] or after the adjective with 'so' ['so formidable a challenge']).

A1_A2.pedagogical_function: Adds a descriptive detail with its own noun and -ing/-ed word to paint a clearer picture of the scene.
A1_A2.imitation_example: The rain having stopped, the students walked out onto the sunny sports field.
A1_A2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Absolute Constructions): Learners frequently join an independent clause with a comma instead of using a participle when there is no conjunction: "[INCORRECT: The bell rang, the students entered -> CORRECT: The bell having rung, the students entered / When the bell rang, the students entered] the classroom."

B1_B2.pedagogical_function: Attaches a non-finite clause with its own explicit subject ('[NP] + [V-ing/V-ed/Adj], [Main Clause]') to depict an accompanying detail or causal circumstance.
B1_B2.imitation_example: All safety inspections completed ahead of schedule, the engineering crew opened the bridge to commuter traffic.
B1_B2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Nominative Absolute vs. Comma Splice): Learners frequently insert a finite verb ('was/were/had') inside an absolute phrase that lacks a conjunction: "[INCORRECT: The funding was approved, the lab ordered -> CORRECT: The funding having been approved / With the funding approved, the lab ordered] the new testing equipment." (Note: Without a conjunction like 'because/after/and', the secondary clause must use a non-finite participle, not a finite verb).

C1_C2.pedagogical_function: Deploys a nominative absolute construction ('[Subordinate NP] + [Participle/Adj/PrepP]') to compress an independent causal condition or descriptive zoom-in without finite subordination.
C1_C2.imitation_example: Major cosmetic houses having capitulated to public pressure, regulatory agencies accelerated the validation of non-animal assays.
C1_C2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Pronoun Case & Non-Finite Predication in Nominative Absolutes): Learners frequently use objective pronoun case or finite verbs in formal nominative absolutes: "[INCORRECT: Them having secured bipartisan backing -> CORRECT: They having secured bipartisan backing / Having secured bipartisan backing], the coalition introduced the regulatory bill." (Note: In a nominative absolute, the overt subject takes the nominative case and governs a non-finite participle; if the subject is identical to the matrix subject, omit the pronoun entirely to form a standard participial adjunct).

A1_A2.pedagogical_function: Highlights key information and creates clear contrast to make sentences more memorable.
A1_A2.imitation_example: The event highlights not just athletic skill, but also warm friendship across cultures.
A1_A2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Emphasis & Symmetry): Learners frequently break parallel structure when linking emphasized phrases: "The festival celebrates not only [INCORRECT: traditional music, but also dancing -> CORRECT: traditional music, but also folk dance]." (Note: Keep coordinated phrases in the same grammatical form).

B1_B2.pedagogical_function: Uses structural symmetry, fronting, or contrastive pairing to highlight the decisive claim in a paragraph.
B1_B2.imitation_example: Effective leadership relies not on unilateral authority, but on transparent communication and shared accountability.
B1_B2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Rhetorical Parallelism): Learners frequently mix clause and phrase categories across contrastive coordinators: "The initiative aims not at [INCORRECT: cutting short-term costs, but to build -> CORRECT: cutting short-term costs, but at building] long-term resilience." (Note: Maintain identical prepositional and non-finite structures across contrastive pairs).

C1_C2.pedagogical_function: Manipulates canonical word order and symmetrical coordination to foreground focal arguments and sharpen dialectical contrast.
C1_C2.imitation_example: Enduring institutional reform arises not from sporadic public outrage, but from the sustained alignment of ethical principle and regulatory design.
C1_C2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Structural Isomorphism in Emphatic Constructions): Learners frequently violate syntactic symmetry or omit obligatory operator inversion in fronted emphatic frames: "Rarely [INCORRECT: public policy shifts -> CORRECT: does public policy shift] without both empirical evidence and organized civic pressure." (Note: Fronted restrictive operators require auxiliary inversion, and antithetical coordinates require strict category matching).

A1_A2.pedagogical_function: Sets clear conditions, reasons, or contrasts so ideas connect logically from one clause to the next.
A1_A2.imitation_example: Although the morning bus was crowded, everyone arrived at the volunteer center on time.
A1_A2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Logical Connectors): Learners frequently combine 'although' and 'but', or 'because' and 'so' in the same sentence: "Although the task was difficult, [INCORRECT: but the team finished -> CORRECT: the team finished] it on time." (Note: Use only one conjunction to link a subordinate clause and a main clause).

B1_B2.pedagogical_function: Signals explicit conditional, concessive, or evidential relationships between clauses to build a balanced argument.
B1_B2.imitation_example: While initial transition costs remain high, long-term energy savings justify the municipal investment.
B1_B2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Logical Subordinators vs. Conjunctive Adverbs): Learners frequently join two independent clauses with ', however,' (comma splice) or follow 'despite' with a finite clause: "The trial showed promising results[INCORRECT: , however, larger studies -> CORRECT: ; however, larger studies] are needed to confirm long-term safety." (Note: Separate independent clauses before 'however/therefore' with a semicolon or period).

C1_C2.pedagogical_function: Calibrates epistemic modality, concessive counter-argumentation, and conditional contingencies in formal academic discourse.
C1_C2.imitation_example: Whereas classical utilitarianism aggregates outcomes across individuals, rights-based ethics establishes inviolable protections for each sentient subject.
C1_C2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Concessive & Evidential Subordination): Learners frequently conflate prepositional concessives ('despite/notwithstanding') with clausal subordinators ('although/whereas') or misapply subjunctive mood in epistemic 'that'-clauses: "[INCORRECT: Notwithstanding that the statute was amended -> CORRECT: Notwithstanding the amendment to the statute / Although the statute was amended], enforcement mechanisms remained uneven." (Note: Match each logical connector to its licensed complement type—NP vs. finite clause).

A1_A2.pedagogical_function: Connects clauses smoothly across ideas and introduces facts or explanations naturally.
A1_A2.imitation_example: The idea that small daily habits can protect the earth is shared by all the students.
A1_A2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Noun Complementation): Learners frequently confuse appositive 'that'-clauses with relative 'which'-clauses: "The news [INCORRECT: which our team won -> CORRECT: that our team won] made everyone cheerful." (Note: Use 'that' when the following clause is complete and states the exact content of the noun).

B1_B2.pedagogical_function: Links propositions across clause boundaries using shell nouns ('the fact/idea that...') or sentential relative clauses (', which...').
B1_B2.imitation_example: The realization that urban heat islands intensify summer energy demand prompted cities to expand tree canopies.
B1_B2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Propositional Framing & Anaphoric Reference): Learners frequently use ', that' or ', what' instead of ', which' to comment on a whole preceding clause: "The district expanded bike lanes by forty kilometers, [INCORRECT: what reduced -> CORRECT: which reduced] morning traffic congestion." (Note: Only ', which' can encapsulate an entire preceding clause as its antecedent).

C1_C2.pedagogical_function: Synthesizes multi-clause argumentation through shell-noun nominalization and anaphoric propositional encapsulation, maintaining tight thematic progression.
C1_C2.imitation_example: The recognition that physiological stress distorts animal bioassays has accelerated the adoption of human-derived organoid models.
C1_C2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Shell-Noun Apposition & Prepositional Complement Constraints): Learners frequently attach a bare 'that'-clause directly to a preposition or replace appositive 'that' with 'which': "Critics challenged the premise [INCORRECT: on that the regulation was built / which animal models are infallible -> CORRECT: on which the regulation was built / that animal models are infallible]." (Note: Use 'that' for complete appositive content clauses, and 'Preposition + which' for gapped relative clauses).

A1_A2.pedagogical_function: Packs multiple descriptive details into a single sentence cleanly without feeling wordy.
A1_A2.imitation_example: Careful planning ensures that the school event runs smoothly and on time.
A1_A2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Syntactic Packaging): Learners frequently mismanage clause boundaries or subject-verb agreement in longer sentences: "Working together in small groups [INCORRECT: help -> CORRECT: helps] shy students speak up with confidence." (Note: A singular gerund or noun head requires a singular verb).

B1_B2.pedagogical_function: Condenses background actions, attributes, and qualifications into non-finite phrases or compact complement frames.
B1_B2.imitation_example: Equipped with real-time air-quality sensors, neighborhood schools can adjust outdoor activity schedules automatically.
B1_B2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Non-Finite Subject Control & Clause Integration): Learners frequently leave participial modifiers unanchored to the main clause subject: "[INCORRECT: Designed to reduce plastic waste, customers can refill containers at the station -> CORRECT: Designed to reduce plastic waste, the station allows customers to refill containers]." (Note: Ensure the noun immediately following a fronted modifier is the entity it describes).

C1_C2.pedagogical_function: Integrates subordinate propositions via non-finite participial adjuncts, absolute constructions, and complex-transitive predication to maximize informational density.
C1_C2.imitation_example: Combining high-throughput cellular screening with computational modeling, toxicologists can evaluate thousands of compounds without animal subjects.
C1_C2.common_mistakes: Grammar Warning (Non-Finite Dependency & Matrix Predication): Learners frequently mismatch voice or subject control when stacking non-finite adjuncts in complex sentences: "[INCORRECT: Having validated across multiple laboratories, the new assay replaced -> CORRECT: Having been validated across multiple laboratories, the new assay replaced] legacy animal tests." (Note: When the matrix subject undergoes the prior action, use the passive perfect participle 'Having been + V-ed').
